svg.aria-label: How Cognito issues signed tokens and how services verify them offline with JWKS
svg.title: How Cognito tokens work — sign in once, verify anywhere
svg.text: How Cognito tokens work — sign in once, verify anywhere
Cognito authenticates the user once and hands back signed tokens. After that, each service checks the token itself, with public keys — no call back to Cognito per request.

THREE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS — AND WHO ANSWERS EACH
Authentication
Who are you?
Answered once, by Cognito, using a password.
Output: a signed ID token.
Strobe: the A1 auth Lambda → Cognito InitiateAuth.
Verification
Is this token genuine and current?
Answered by every service, offline, with public keys.
No shared secret and no session table to look up.
Strobe: API Gateway, auth.ts, FastMCP JWTVerifier.
Authorization
What may this user touch?
Answered by your own code, using the verified sub.
Cognito knows nothing about posts or photos.
Strobe: filter userId = sub; post.userId == sub.
The trade-off of stateless tokens
Because nobody asks Cognito per request, a service cannot see a sign-out: a leaked ID token stays valid until its exp. That is why ID and access
tokens are short-lived (Cognito default: 60 minutes) and a long-lived refresh token, which Cognito CAN revoke, is used to get new ones.
